etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English mete, from Old English mete (“food”), from Proto-West Germanic *mati, from Proto-Germanic *matiz (“food”), from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to drip, ooze; grease, fat”). Cognate with West Frisian mete, Old Saxon meti, Old High German maz (“food”), Icelandic matur, Swedish mat, Gothic 𐌼𐌰𐍄𐍃 (mats).

A -ja- derivation from the same base is found in Middle Dutch and Middle Low German met (“lean pork”), from which Dutch met (“minced pork”) and German Mett (“minced meat”) derive, respectively. Compare also Old Irish mess (“animal feed”) and Welsh mes (“acorns”), English mast (“fodder for swine and other animals”), which are probably from the same root.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The flesh (muscle tissue) of an animal used as food. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1983, Richard Ellis, The Book of Sharks, Knopf, →ISBN, page 144:
quote.text: In many parts of the world, shark meat is an acceptable and desirable form of protein.

quote.citation: 2010 October 19, Andy Atkins, “Debate on meat-eating does not cut the mustard”, in The Guardian‎[1]:
quote.text: While people who eat no meat at all are identified and identifiable as vegetarians, there is no commonly accepted term for people who eat it only a couple of times a week and are selective about its quality.

definitions.definition: (countable) A type of meat, by anatomic position and provenance. [from 16th c.]
(now archaic, dialectal) Food, for animals or humans, especially solid food. See also meat and drink. [from 8th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Matthew:
quote.text: I was anhongred, and ye gave me meate. I thursted, and ye gave me drinke.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 8, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC, page 232:
quote.text: And he was pleased to accompany them in their death; for, he pined away by abstaining from all manner of meat.

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, (please specify the act number in uppercase Roman numerals, and the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals):
quote.text: Your greatest want is, you want much of meat: / Why should you want? Behold, the Earth hath Rootes […].
As full of fun and frolic as an egg is full of meat.

quote.citation: 1936, Djuna Barnes, Nightwood, Faber & Faber, published 2007, page 13:
quote.text: The way she said ‘dinner’ and the way she said ‘champagne’ gave meat and liquid their exact difference […].

definitions.definition: (now rare) A type of food, a dish. [from 9th c.]

quote.citation: 1526, [William Tyndale, transl.], The Newe Testamẽt […] (Tyndale Bible), [Worms, Germany: Peter Schöffer], →OCLC, Matthew viij:
quote.text: And hit cam to passe, thatt Jesus satt at meate in his housse.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Any relatively thick, solid part of a fruit, nut etc. [from 15th c.]

quote.text: She took her spoon and stirred the melted butter into the yellow meat of the yam.

definitions.definition: (colloquial) The best or most substantial part of something. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1577, Gerald Eades Bentley, The Arte of Angling:
quote.text: […] it is time to begin "A Dialogue between Viator and Piscator," which is the meat of the matter.

definitions.definition: (sports) The sweet spot of a bat or club (in cricket, golf, baseball etc.). [from 20th c.]
(Australian Aboriginal) A totem, or (by metonymy) a clan or clansman which uses it.

quote.text: When a stranger comes to an aboriginal camp or settlement in north-western NSW, he is asked by one of the older aborigines: "What meat (clan) are you?"
Granny Sullivan was ‘dead against’ the match at first because they did not know "what my meat was and because I was a bit on the fair side."

quote.citation: 1977, A. K. Eckermann, Group Organisation and Identity:
quote.text: Some people maintained that she was "sung" because her family had killed or eaten the "meat" (totem) of another group.

quote.citation: 1992, P. Taylor, Tell it Like it Is:
quote.text: Our family […] usually married the red kangaroo "meat".
That’s a beautiful goanna. […]. He’s my meat, can’t eat him.
